title: Did anyone see it in early previews AND after the cuts? #broadway #mu...
transcript: A surprise pregnancy, a lawsuit, one of the most stacked Broadway casts in recent memory, and there's *still* so much more to say about this show. I knew I'd have to talk about this eventually, and with the anniversary concert just announced, I think it's finally time. So strap in and welcome to another episode of Overthinking Theatre Throwback, where I do retrospectives on recent theatre history. On March 15th, 2016, I waited in the rush line for a mysterious new Broadway show. A rare musical that opened without any pre Broadway tryout. But the cast included, and listen closely here: Audra McDonald, Brian Stokes Mitchell, Joshua Henry, Billy Porter, Brandon Victor Dixon, Adrienne Warren, Amber Iman, and Brooks Ashmanskas playing all the white people like, are you freaking kidding me? Written and directed by the legendary George C. Wolfe, it was called Shuffle Along, or the making of the Musical Sensation of 1921 and all that Followed. And as the lengthy title suggested, it told the true behind the scenes story of the 1921 musical Shuffle Along, which was a landmark moment for black representation on Broadway. I managed to get my rush ticket to the first preview, and as we walked into the theater, we could hear from behind the curtain the sound of a single tap dancer; a little taste of what was to come in this singular theatrical experience. A few months later, I told my friend that I attended this first preview, and he joked, “are you sure you aren’t *still* at that first preview?” With a run time of about 3 hours and 15 minutes, not including the late start, it was bloated, messy, and threw everything to the wall to see what stuck. And yet it was a beautiful, exhilarating mess with some of the best tap choreography I've ever seen. Possibly my biggest issue with it is that the book still felt, on a structural level, like it was using the bio jukebox musical formula. The pre existing songs by Sissle and Blake didn't always mesh in the narrative. And it relied a little too much on historical narration, especially in the second act, which crammed in a huge amount of plot. But, of course, it was doing something the rest of the bio jukebox musicals weren't: It was shedding light on this important chapter of history and doing it with a lot of artful flair, but also, pivotally setting them apart from most new musicals, they actually use their preview period to make massive changes. I made a video last year theorizing that a lot of the discourse around Broadway previews stems from the fact that artists and audiences experience it very differently. But this was a rare case where audience word of mouth noticeably improved throughout previews. And they did that by doing what most musicals won't. They took a brief hiatus in the middle of previews to implement major cuts. They even cut an entire role in early previews. There was a recurring side character who was later revealed to be Josephine Baker, but that whole arc was cut and so the actor playing her, Felicia Boswell, was unfortunately let go. Also cut was a deeply haunting Act 2 number where Brian Stokes Mitchell's character had like a mental breakdown singing a reprise of the title song with black face makeup on only half his face. It was this sort of “bonus material” that made me glad I attended the first preview. But it did seem like the people who saw the tightened version got a better show overall. I actually intended to go back and see it again, but that brings us to the unfortunate drama surrounding this production. They got nominated for an impressive 10 Tony Awards, but they had the misfortune of going up against a little juggernaut called Hamilton. Producer, Scott Rudin, tried to circumvent this with some of his usual nonsense by petitioning to count it as a revival, but calling this a revival of the original Shuffle Along is laughably inaccurate by any reasonable metric. It's not even an adaptation, as some of the marketing tried to position it, and appropriately, this desperate ploy failed. It was also a particularly strong year in the actress category, to the point where Audra McDonald, fresh off back to back wins, didn't even get nominated. They even got unlucky in the choreography category with an unusually strong set of nominees. Although I still think they should have beat Hamilton. All that to say left without any Tony wins, the production began to worry for its longevity, particularly because by this point Audra McDonald had announced she was pregnant. She already had a pre-planned absence to do a run of Lady Day in London and return to the production 3 months later, but that was no longer on the table. Acclaimed folk musician Rhiannon Giddens had been cast as her replacement. Also, Savion Glover, tap icon and the show's choreographer, was going to join the cast in a new featured ensemble track designed to highlight his skills, and it was after these changeovers that I was planning to revisit the show. Audra famously continued in the show for as long as possible, with some of the choreography tailored to accommodate her impressively advanced stage of pregnancy, and audiences, just happy to see her, rightfully suspended their disbelief as she played this clearly not pregnant character. Audra had to leave eventually, and apparently Giddens and Glover were not moving tickets as they hoped, and while the production might have been able to weather that for a finite three month absence, the new circumstances were harder to plan for. Rudin decided to close the production when McDonald left, cancelling Giddens’ and Glover's engagement entirely. But the drama had only just started. Despite some legitimate concerns around ticket sales, it did seem from the outside like Rudin was using the specific timing as an attempt to cash in on the show's insurance policy, claiming McDonald's pregnancy as a case of illness or accident, but Rudin sued the insurance company when they refused to cover the claim, saying that McDonald was in control of whether she got pregnant or not, therefore it didn't count as an illness or accident. This dragged on for some time, but they dropped the suit in 2020. And it is a shame that this drama seemed to overshadow both the brilliance of the musical and this otherwise very happy event in McDonald and Swenson's life. But the show did close, and likely because of their financial situation, it was the rare new Broadway musical that didn't even get a cast album, leaving it up to those of us who saw it to recall this musical sensation of 2016 and all that followed.
